questions.title: Muscle that unlocks the knee
questions.question: Unlocking of the fully extended knee, before flexion can begin, is mainly done by:

explanations.A: Correct. Popliteus arises from the lateral femoral condyle and inserts on the posterior tibia; contracting, it laterally rotates the femur on the fixed tibia, reversing the screw-home mechanism that locked the knee. It must act first, before the hamstrings can produce any flexion at all. A popliteus that cannot function leaves a knee that cannot begin to bend, however strong the hamstrings are.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Biceps femoris is a hamstring that flexes the already-unlocked knee; it plays no part in the initial unlocking rotation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Quadratus femoris is a lateral rotator of the hip joint and has no action at the knee at all.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Gastrocnemius crosses the knee and weakly assists flexion once it is unlocked, and plantarflexes the ankle, but it is not the muscle responsible for the unlocking rotation itself.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Plantaris is a vestigial muscle contributing weakly to knee flexion and ankle plantarflexion; it has no unlocking role.

questions.learning_objective: Identify popliteus as the muscle that unlocks the fully extended knee.

questions.title: Insertion of the superficial posterior compartment
questions.question: All muscles of the superficial posterior compartment of the leg insert into:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The fibula receives muscles of the lateral and deep posterior compartments (peroneus longus/brevis, part of soleus's origin), not the insertion of the superficial group.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The talus has no muscular insertions at all — tendons cross it but attach elsewhere, chiefly the calcaneus and navicular.
explanations.C: Correct. Gastrocnemius, soleus and plantaris all converge on the tendo calcaneus (Achilles tendon), which inserts on the posterior surface of the calcaneus. This shared insertion is why all three act, directly or indirectly, to plantarflex the ankle at the subtalar/calcaneal lever.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The first metatarsal receives tibialis anterior and part of peroneus longus, both from other compartments, not the superficial posterior group.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The cuboid receives no superficial posterior compartment muscle; peroneus longus's tendon merely grooves it en route to the first metatarsal/medial cuneiform.

questions.learning_objective: State that gastrocnemius, soleus and plantaris all insert via the tendo calcaneus onto the calcaneus.

questions.title: Anterior tibial nerve position at the ankle
questions.question: While passing deep to the superior extensor retinaculum, the anterior tibial (deep peroneal) nerve lies medial to:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Extensor hallucis longus lies medial to the neurovascular bundle at this level, not lateral to it — so the nerve is lateral to, not medial to, extensor hallucis longus.
explanations.B: Correct. From medial to lateral at the ankle the order is: tibialis anterior tendon, extensor hallucis longus tendon, anterior tibial vessels with the deep peroneal nerve, then extensor digitorum longus tendon and peroneus tertius. The deep peroneal nerve therefore lies medial to extensor digitorum longus.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Tibialis anterior's tendon is the most medial structure at this level, well medial to the nerve, not lateral to it.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The anterior tibial artery runs immediately alongside the deep peroneal nerve as a paired neurovascular bundle, not as a separate structure the nerve sits medial to.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Peroneus tertius is the most lateral tendon at the ankle, well lateral to the nerve — the nerve's medial relation is to extensor digitorum longus, which lies between it and peroneus tertius.

questions.learning_objective: State the medial-to-lateral order of tendons and neurovascular structures deep to the superior extensor retinaculum.

questions.title: Dorsiflexors of the foot
questions.question: All of the following muscles are dorsiflexors of the foot EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (it IS a dorsiflexor). Peroneus tertius, part of the anterior compartment, dorsiflexes and everts the ankle.
explanations.B: Incorrect (it IS a dorsiflexor). Tibialis anterior is the prime mover of dorsiflexion, also inverting the foot.
explanations.C: Incorrect (it IS a dorsiflexor). Extensor hallucis longus dorsiflexes the ankle as it extends the great toe.
explanations.D: Correct. Peroneus longus is a lateral compartment muscle, supplied by the superficial peroneal nerve, that plantarflexes and everts the foot. It is not a dorsiflexor, unlike the other three anterior-compartment options. Its tendon crosses the sole to attach near the base of the first metatarsal, powering eversion and supporting the transverse arch, actions unrelated to dorsiflexion.

questions.learning_objective: List the anterior compartment's dorsiflexors and distinguish them from the lateral compartment's plantarflexor/evertor, peroneus longus.

questions.title: Tibial nerve supply — the hamstring exception
questions.question: All of the following muscles are supplied by the tibial (medial popliteal) nerve EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Correct. The short head of biceps femoris is the one hamstring supplied by the common peroneal division of the sciatic nerve rather than the tibial division — it acts only at the knee and is the classic exception that survives a tibial-division-selective sciatic injury. This division-based split is the standard way this bank distinguishes a proximal (undivided) sciatic injury, which paralyses all hamstrings, from a more distal tibial-division lesion, which spares this one muscle.
explanations.B: Incorrect (it IS tibial-supplied). Gastrocnemius is a superficial posterior compartment muscle, supplied throughout by the tibial nerve.
explanations.C: Incorrect (it IS tibial-supplied). Soleus is likewise supplied by the tibial nerve.
explanations.D: Incorrect (it IS tibial-supplied). Plantaris, the third superficial posterior compartment muscle, is also tibial-nerve-supplied.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the short head of biceps femoris as the one hamstring supplied by the common peroneal, not tibial, division of the sciatic nerve.

questions.title: What does not pass deep to the extensor retinaculum
questions.question: All of the following pass deep to the superior extensor retinaculum of the foot EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (it DOES pass deep to it). The deep peroneal (anterior tibial) nerve runs with the anterior tibial vessels deep to the superior extensor retinaculum.
explanations.B: Incorrect (it DOES pass deep to it). Peroneus tertius's tendon, the most lateral of the group, also passes deep to the retinaculum.
explanations.C: Incorrect (it DOES pass deep to it). Tibialis anterior's tendon, the most medial, likewise passes deep to the retinaculum.
explanations.D: Correct. Flexor hallucis longus is a deep posterior compartment muscle whose tendon runs behind the medial malleolus into the sole, not through the anterior extensor retinaculum at all — a classic trap for extensor hallucis longus, which is the tendon actually found there. Extensor hallucis longus's tendon lies between tibialis anterior and the anterior tibial vessels at this level, and it is the tendon a student should name here instead.

questions.learning_objective: Distinguish the four structures deep to the superior extensor retinaculum from flexor hallucis longus, a deep posterior compartment tendon that does not pass there.

questions.title: Dorsiflexion and eversion together
questions.question: Which ONE of the following muscles is responsible for dorsiflexion AND eversion of the foot?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Tibialis anterior dorsiflexes and inverts the foot, not everts it.
explanations.B: Correct. Peroneus tertius is anatomically part of the anterior compartment (deep-peroneal-supplied, dorsiflexor) despite functioning like a lateral-compartment evertor, so it uniquely combines dorsiflexion with eversion. The other anterior compartment muscles (tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis longus) dorsiflex but invert rather than evert, so peroneus tertius is the one exception worth memorising deliberately.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Peroneus longus everts the foot but plantarflexes it, the opposite of dorsiflexion.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Flexor digitorum longus plantarflexes and inverts the foot while flexing the lateral four toes; it has no dorsiflexion or eversion action.

questions.learning_objective: Identify peroneus tertius as the muscle combining dorsiflexion with eversion, unlike the other named leg muscles.

questions.hold: flawed source item — three of the four options (flexor digitorum longus, soleus, tibialis posterior) are all genuinely innervated by the tibial/medial popliteal nerve; only peroneus brevis is distinguishable as wrong. Confirmed against the rendered page (p3): no dropped negation in the stem. Cannot honestly write a false distractor-teaching-sentence for two options that are anatomically correct alongside the printed key (B, soleus).

questions.title: Muscle most related to the medial malleolus
questions.question: Which of the following muscles is most related to the medial malleolus?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Soleus inserts via the tendo calcaneus onto the calcaneus, not passing behind the medial malleolus.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Plantaris likewise joins the tendo calcaneus and has no relation to the medial malleolus.
explanations.C: Correct. Tibialis posterior's tendon is the most anterior of the deep posterior compartment tendons passing immediately behind the medial malleolus (order, anterior to posterior: tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus, posterior tibial vessels/tibial nerve, flexor hallucis longus), making it the tendon most closely related to that landmark. A student locating the medial malleolus surgically or on imaging should expect tibialis posterior's tendon to be the first one encountered immediately behind it.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Peroneus tertius is an anterior compartment tendon at the front of the ankle, unrelated to the medial malleolus.

questions.learning_objective: State that tibialis posterior's tendon is the deep posterior compartment tendon most closely related to the medial malleolus.

questions.title: Weakness in dorsiflexion and inversion
questions.question: A patient experiences weakness in dorsiflexing and inverting the foot. Which of the following muscles is damaged?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Fibularis (peroneus) longus everts and plantarflexes the foot, the opposite pair of actions.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Fibularis brevis also everts (and weakly plantarflexes) the foot.
explanations.C: Correct. Tibialis anterior is the only muscle that both dorsiflexes and inverts the foot together, so weakness in exactly that combination points to it. Because tibialis anterior is the only muscle producing exactly that combination, this stem is a reliable single-answer test of the dorsiflexion-inversion pairing.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Extensor digitorum longus dorsiflexes and helps evert the foot while extending the lateral four toes — it does not invert.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Fibularis (peroneus) tertius dorsiflexes and everts, again the wrong combination.

questions.learning_objective: Identify tibialis anterior as the sole muscle combining dorsiflexion with inversion.

questions.title: Artery at risk with a fibular neck fracture
questions.question: A 20-year-old footballer sustains a fracture of the head and neck of the fibula. Which of the following arteries could also be damaged by this fracture?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The popliteal artery lies proximal to and deep within the popliteal fossa, well away from the fibular neck itself.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The posterior tibial artery descends deep to soleus on the posteromedial leg, not at the fibular neck.
explanations.C: Correct. The anterior tibial artery pierces the interosseous membrane close to the fibular neck to enter the anterior compartment, putting it directly in the path of a fibular-neck fracture, alongside the common peroneal nerve wrapped around the same bony point. Both structures cross the interosseous membrane/wind around the fibular neck at essentially the same point, which is why this fracture is classically taught as a combined nerve-and-vessel injury.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The peroneal artery runs in the deep posterior compartment near the fibula's shaft, not specifically exposed at the neck the way the anterior tibial artery is as it crosses the interosseous membrane there.

questions.learning_objective: Explain why the anterior tibial artery, crossing the interosseous membrane near the fibular neck, is vulnerable in a fibular neck fracture alongside the common peroneal nerve.

questions.title: A muscle acting on two joints
questions.question: Which of the following muscles can act on 2 joints?

explanations.A: Correct. Gastrocnemius arises above the knee from the femoral condyles, so it crosses both the knee (weak flexor) and the ankle (strong plantarflexor), making it biarticular. This is functionally important: gastrocnemius's knee-flexion contribution is lost when the knee is already fully flexed (active insufficiency), which is why it is a much weaker knee flexor than a true hamstring.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Popliteus acts only at the knee, rotating the femur on the tibia to unlock it.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Soleus arises below the knee from the tibia/fibula and acts only at the ankle, plantarflexing it.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Pectineus is a hip muscle (flexor/adductor) acting at a single joint, the hip; it is not even a leg muscle.

questions.learning_objective: Identify gastrocnemius as biarticular, crossing both the knee and the ankle, unlike soleus.

questions.title: Skin of the lateral foot border
questions.question: The skin on the lateral border of the foot up to the tip of the little toe is supplied by:

explanations.A: Correct. The sural nerve, passing behind the lateral malleolus with the small saphenous vein, continues along the lateral border of the foot to the little toe — its signature territory in this bank. Because it lies close to the small saphenous vein throughout, the sural nerve is also the classic site for a nerve biopsy, since its loss costs only this tolerable strip of numbness.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The saphenous nerve covers the medial leg down to the medial malleolus and does not reach the foot at all, let alone the lateral border.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The superficial peroneal nerve covers the dorsum of the foot generally, but the specific lateral-border-to-little-toe strip belongs to the sural nerve.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The lateral plantar nerve supplies the sole, not the dorsal/lateral skin border being asked about here.

questions.learning_objective: State that the sural nerve supplies the lateral border of the foot to the little toe.

questions.title: Cutaneous supply of the anteromedial leg
questions.question: The cutaneous supply of the anteromedial side of the leg is provided by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The obturator nerve's cutaneous branch covers only a small patch of the medial thigh, well proximal to the leg.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The sural nerve covers the posterolateral, not anteromedial, leg.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The superficial peroneal nerve covers the anterolateral leg, the opposite side from the one asked about.
explanations.D: Correct. The saphenous nerve, the sensory continuation of the femoral nerve, runs down the medial side of the leg to the medial malleolus, covering the anteromedial skin asked about here. Because it runs with the great saphenous vein, the saphenous nerve is also at risk during varicose vein stripping surgery in this region.

questions.learning_objective: State that the saphenous nerve supplies the anteromedial skin of the leg.

questions.title: Nerve responsible for knee extension
questions.question: Difficulty in extending the knee can result from damage to:

explanations.A: Correct. The femoral nerve supplies quadriceps femoris, the sole extensor of the knee, so its injury directly impairs knee extension. Quadriceps femoris (rectus femoris and the three vasti) is the only knee extensor, so no other named nerve in this list can substitute for the femoral nerve here.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The tibial nerve supplies the posterior compartment (knee flexors and ankle plantarflexors/invertors), not the extensor.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The sural nerve is purely sensory (lower posterolateral leg and lateral foot) and has no motor role at the knee.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The obturator nerve supplies the hip adductors and a small sensory patch of the medial thigh, not the knee extensors.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The common peroneal nerve supplies the anterior/lateral leg compartments (foot dorsiflexors/evertors), not the thigh's knee extensor.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the femoral nerve as supplying quadriceps femoris, the knee's only extensor.

questions.title: Sciatic injury and spared sensation
questions.question: If the sciatic nerve was injured by an intramuscular gluteal injection, the patient would have diminished cutaneous sensation on:

explanations.A: Correct. The dorsum of the foot is superficial peroneal nerve territory, a sciatic-nerve derivative, so a sciatic injury reduces its sensation. This is exactly why a sciatic-level lesion (from a gluteal injection) can be distinguished from a lower motor neuron lesion of a purely distal nerve — the medial leg's sparing is the diagnostic clue.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this territory is spared). The medial side of the leg is saphenous nerve territory, a femoral-nerve derivative unrelated to the sciatic nerve, so it is not affected.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Because the medial leg (saphenous/femoral) is spared, only the dorsum of the foot, not both areas, loses sensation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The dorsum of the foot does lose sensation, so "neither" is wrong.

questions.learning_objective: Use the saphenous (femoral-derived, spared) versus superficial peroneal (sciatic-derived, lost) territories to localise a sciatic nerve injury.

questions.title: Sensory loss from a tibial nerve injury
questions.question: Tibial nerve injury may lead to loss of sensation in:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The anterolateral leg is superficial peroneal territory, not tibial.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The posteromedial leg above the ankle is largely saphenous (femoral-derived) territory, not tibial.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The dorsum of the foot is superficial (and, in the first web space, deep) peroneal territory, not tibial.
explanations.D: Correct. The sole of the foot is supplied by the tibial nerve's medial and lateral plantar branches, so it alone is lost with a tibial nerve injury. Recognising this narrow, single territory prevents a student from over-attributing more widespread leg sensory loss to the tibial nerve alone.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Since A, B and C are not tibial territory, "all of the above" overstates the tibial nerve's actual cutaneous field.

questions.learning_objective: Restrict the tibial nerve's cutaneous territory to the sole of the foot alone.

questions.title: Sciatic nerve injury and foot movement
questions.question: Injury of the sciatic nerve can lead to severe impairment in:

explanations.A: Incorrect alone. Inversion and dorsiflexion (tibialis anterior, deep peroneal territory) is impaired, but so are the movements in the other options, since the sciatic nerve gives rise to both its tibial and common peroneal divisions.
explanations.B: Incorrect alone. Eversion and dorsiflexion (common peroneal territory) is also impaired, alongside the movements in the other options.
explanations.C: Incorrect alone. Inversion and plantarflexion (tibial territory) is also impaired, alongside the other options.
explanations.D: Correct. The sciatic nerve gives rise to both the tibial division (plantarflexion, inversion) and the common peroneal division (dorsiflexion, eversion), so a proximal sciatic injury impairs every one of these movements together, not any single pair alone. This is the key reasoning step distinguishing a proximal sciatic lesion (all foot movements impaired) from an isolated tibial or common peroneal lesion (only half the movements impaired).

questions.learning_objective: Explain why a proximal sciatic nerve injury impairs the full range of foot movements, since it carries both the tibial and common peroneal divisions.

questions.title: Tibial nerve relation to the popliteal artery
questions.question: In the upper part of the popliteal fossa, the tibial nerve lies ......... to the popliteal artery.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Neither structure lies simply anterior to the other in this plane; the relevant relation the bank tests is medial-lateral, not anteroposterior.
explanations.B: Incorrect, for the same reason — the tested relation here is medial-lateral, not anteroposterior.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The popliteal artery, not the tibial nerve, is the medial (and deepest) of the three main popliteal-fossa structures at this level.
explanations.D: Correct. At the upper part of the popliteal fossa the tibial nerve is the most superficial and lateral of the three neurovascular structures, with the popliteal vein intermediate and the popliteal artery deepest and most medial against the femur. This lateral position makes the tibial nerve the structure most exposed to injury during posterior knee surgery, before the deeper vein and artery are reached.

questions.learning_objective: State that the tibial nerve lies lateral to the popliteal artery in the upper part of the popliteal fossa.

questions.title: Sensory loss from a femoral nerve injury
questions.question: Injury of the femoral nerve leads to loss of sensation in:

explanations.A: Incorrect alone. The anterior thigh (anterior cutaneous nerves of the thigh) is femoral territory, but so are the other listed areas.
explanations.B: Incorrect alone. Part of the medial thigh is also femoral (intermediate cutaneous nerve) territory, alongside the other listed areas.
explanations.C: Incorrect alone. The medial border of the foot, via the saphenous nerve (the femoral nerve's long sensory continuation), is also femoral territory.
explanations.D: Correct. The femoral nerve's cutaneous branches together cover the front of the thigh, part of the medial thigh, and — via the saphenous nerve running all the way to the foot — the medial leg and the medial border of the foot, so all three areas lose sensation with a femoral nerve injury. Recognising the saphenous nerve as the femoral nerve's distal continuation is what links an apparently thigh-only nerve to sensory loss as far away as the foot.

questions.learning_objective: Trace the femoral nerve's sensory field from the anterior/medial thigh down the saphenous nerve to the medial foot border.

questions.title: Nerve for hip extension and lateral rotation
questions.question: Injury of which nerve causes impairment in hip extension and lateral rotation?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The sciatic nerve itself does not supply gluteus maximus; it passes near it but the extensor/lateral rotator is separately innervated.
explanations.B: Correct. The inferior gluteal nerve supplies gluteus maximus, the main extensor and a lateral rotator of the hip, so its injury impairs exactly those two actions. Because gluteus maximus is the prime hip extensor and a lateral rotator, the inferior gluteal nerve is the single nerve whose loss reproduces exactly this combination of deficits.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The obturator nerve supplies the hip adductors, not the extensor/lateral rotator.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The posterior tibial (tibial) nerve acts distally on the leg and foot, not on the hip.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the inferior gluteal nerve as supplying gluteus maximus, the hip's extensor and lateral rotator.

questions.title: First web space cutaneous supply
questions.question: The sides of the 1st and 2nd toes on the dorsal surface of the foot are supplied by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The sural nerve covers the lateral foot border to the little toe, not the first web space.
explanations.B: Correct. The deep peroneal nerve, despite driving the whole anterior compartment motor-wise, is reduced cutaneously to exactly this small first-web-space patch between the great and second toes. Recognising this mismatch between the deep peroneal nerve's large motor territory and its tiny sensory territory is a common source of localisation errors if not memorised deliberately.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The saphenous nerve does not reach the toes at all, stopping at the medial malleolus/foot.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The posterior tibial nerve's plantar branches supply the sole, not the dorsal web space.

questions.learning_objective: State that the deep peroneal nerve's cutaneous territory is reduced to the first web space.

questions.title: Sensation spared by a common peroneal injury
questions.question: This patient (with a common peroneal nerve injury from a fibular neck fracture) may lose sensation in all of these areas EXCEPT:

options.D: Lateral side of foot up to little toe

explanations.A: Incorrect (this IS lost). The anterolateral leg is superficial peroneal territory, lost with a common peroneal injury.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this IS lost). The web space between the 4th and 5th toes is superficial peroneal territory, also lost.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this IS lost). The medial side of the big toe is superficial peroneal (dorsal) territory in this bank's scheme, also lost.
explanations.D: Correct. The lateral side of the foot up to the little toe is sural nerve territory — and the sural nerve is not a common peroneal branch, so this strip is spared even though it sits close to the lateral foot the common peroneal nerve otherwise supplies. This is a useful discriminator: a patient whose lateral-foot sensation to the little toe is preserved despite obvious foot drop is showing a pattern consistent with an isolated common peroneal lesion rather than a full sciatic nerve injury.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that the sural nerve's lateral-foot territory is spared by a common peroneal nerve injury despite its proximity.

questions.title: The false statement about the sural nerve
questions.question: All of the following are correct about the sural nerve EXCEPT:

options.A: It supplies the lateral side of the foot up to the little toe
options.B: It passes behind the lateral malleolus
options.C: It is a branch from the common peroneal nerve
options.D: It accompanies the small saphenous vein in its course

explanations.A: Incorrect (this IS true). The sural nerve does supply the lateral foot border to the little toe.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this IS true). It does pass behind the lateral malleolus.
explanations.C: Correct — this is the false statement. The sural nerve is formed mainly from the medial sural cutaneous branch of the tibial nerve. It is joined variably by a peroneal communicating branch from the common peroneal nerve, but it is not simply "a branch from the common peroneal nerve" as this option claims.
explanations.D: Incorrect (this IS true). It does run alongside the small (short) saphenous vein.

questions.learning_objective: State that the sural nerve is chiefly a tibial-nerve derivative (with a peroneal contribution), not simply a common peroneal branch.

questions.title: A true statement about leg nerves
questions.question: Concerning the nerves of the lower limb, which ONE of the following statements is TRUE?

options.B: Superficial peroneal nerve supplies peroneus tertius
options.D: Extensor hallucis longus is supplied by posterior tibial nerve

explanations.A: Correct. Popliteus is part of the deep posterior compartment and, like the rest of that group, is supplied by the tibial nerve. None of the other three named nerve-muscle pairings in this stem is correct, which is what makes this the single true statement among the four.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Peroneus tertius is anatomically part of the anterior compartment and is supplied by the deep peroneal nerve, not the superficial peroneal nerve.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The sural nerve is a purely sensory nerve with no muscular branches at all, let alone to soleus.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Extensor hallucis longus is an anterior compartment muscle supplied by the deep peroneal nerve, not the posterior tibial nerve.

questions.learning_objective: Confirm that popliteus, part of the deep posterior compartment, is tibial-nerve-supplied.

questions.title: Superior gluteal nerve injury — the exception
questions.question: Injury to the superior gluteal nerve will result in the following effects EXCEPT:

options.A: Inability to abduct the thigh at the hip joint

explanations.A: Incorrect (this DOES occur). The superior gluteal nerve supplies the hip abductors, so abduction is impaired.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this DOES occur). Gluteus medius, an abductor supplied by this nerve, is paralysed.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this DOES occur). Loss of gluteus medius/minimus stabilisation produces the classic Trendelenburg sign.
explanations.D: Correct. Hip extension is produced by gluteus maximus via the inferior gluteal nerve, a different nerve entirely — so it is not affected by a superior gluteal nerve injury. Recognising that abduction/Trendelenburg (superior gluteal) and extension (inferior gluteal) are controlled by two separate nerves is the key discriminator this stem tests.

questions.learning_objective: Distinguish the superior gluteal nerve's abductor/Trendelenburg effects from hip extension, which depends on the separate inferior gluteal nerve.

questions.title: A true statement about the anterior tibial nerve
questions.question: Which statement is true about the anterior tibial (deep peroneal) nerve?

options.A: It descends in the leg medial to the anterior tibial artery
options.B: It supplies muscles of the sole of the foot
options.C: It carries the sensation from the whole dorsum of the foot
options.D: It supplies the muscles responsible for dorsiflexing the foot

explanations.A: Incorrect. The nerve's position relative to the artery varies along the leg's course rather than staying fixed medial to it throughout.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The sole's muscles are supplied by the tibial nerve's plantar branches, not the deep peroneal nerve.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The deep peroneal nerve's cutaneous field is only the first web space, not the whole dorsum (which is mostly superficial peroneal territory).
explanations.D: Correct. The deep peroneal nerve supplies the entire anterior compartment — tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis longus, extensor digitorum longus, peroneus tertius — the muscles responsible for dorsiflexing the ankle. None of the deep peroneal nerve's other proposed roles in this stem (sole muscles, whole-dorsum sensation) is correct, leaving dorsiflexion as the one true statement.

questions.learning_objective: Confirm the deep peroneal nerve's motor role driving the whole dorsiflexor group.

questions.title: Sciatic nerve injury — the true statement
questions.question: In case of a complete sciatic nerve injury, which of the following is true?

options.A: The patient loses sensation in the posterior aspect of the thigh
options.B: The patient can only invert the foot, but cannot evert it
options.C: All the hamstring muscles are paralyzed
options.D: The patient loses sensation in the sole of the foot only, but not in the dorsum

explanations.A: Incorrect. The posterior thigh's skin is largely covered by the posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh, a separate branch from the sciatic itself, so this is not the defining true statement here.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A complete sciatic injury removes both inversion (tibial) and eversion (common peroneal), since it damages both divisions together — the patient loses both, not just eversion.
explanations.C: Correct. Because a complete sciatic nerve injury (before the nerve divides) damages both the tibial and common peroneal divisions bundled together, even the short head of biceps femoris (normally spared by a tibial-division-selective lesion) is paralysed, so all hamstrings are affected. This distinction — a proximal sciatic lesion paralysing all hamstrings versus a distal tibial-division lesion sparing the short head of biceps femoris — is a classic localising question in this bank.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Both the sole (tibial) and the dorsum (common peroneal/superficial peroneal) lose sensation with a complete sciatic injury, not the sole alone.

questions.learning_objective: Explain why a complete (undivided) sciatic nerve injury paralyses every hamstring, including the short head of biceps femoris that a more distal, tibial-selective lesion would spare.

questions.title: Unlocking the knee to permit flexion
questions.question: A 34-year-old man has difficulty walking; examination reveals a problem of unlocking the knee to permit flexion of the leg. Which of the following muscles is most likely affected?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Biceps femoris flexes the knee once it is already unlocked; it does not perform the unlocking step itself.
explanations.B: Correct. Popliteus must laterally rotate the femur on the tibia to release the screw-home lock before any knee flexion can occur, exactly the deficit described. Recognising popliteus's unlocking role, rather than assuming hamstring weakness, is the key diagnostic step this vignette is testing.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Gastrocnemius assists flexion weakly once unlocked and plantarflexes the ankle; it does not unlock the joint.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Rectus femoris is a knee extensor (and hip flexor), the opposite action from what is being asked about.

questions.learning_objective: Apply the popliteus-unlocking mechanism to a clinical vignette of a knee that cannot begin to flex.

questions.title: Nerve behind sole sensory loss
questions.question: A 27-year-old patient exhibits a loss of skin sensation on the plantar aspect of the foot following a motorcycle accident. Which of the following nerves is most likely damaged?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The common peroneal nerve and its branches supply the dorsum, not the sole, of the foot.
explanations.B: Correct. The sole of the foot is supplied by the tibial nerve's medial and lateral plantar branches, so plantar sensory loss localises to the tibial nerve. This pattern — plantar sensory loss with preserved dorsal sensation — should point specifically to the tibial nerve rather than a more proximal sciatic lesion, where both surfaces would be affected.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The superficial peroneal nerve covers most of the dorsum, not the sole.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The deep peroneal nerve's cutaneous field is only the first dorsal web space, not the sole.

questions.learning_objective: Localise plantar sensory loss to the tibial nerve's plantar branches.

questions.title: Muscle for plantarflexion and inversion
questions.question: A patient is unable to plantar flex and invert his foot. Which of the following muscles is most likely damaged?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Extensor digitorum longus dorsiflexes and helps evert, the opposite pair of actions.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Tibialis anterior dorsiflexes and inverts — right invertor, wrong direction of ankle movement.
explanations.C: Correct. Tibialis posterior, a deep posterior compartment muscle, both plantarflexes and inverts the foot, matching the deficit exactly. No other listed muscle combines plantarflexion with inversion, which is what makes tibialis posterior the single correct answer.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Peroneus longus plantarflexes but everts, not inverts.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Peroneus brevis likewise plantarflexes and everts, not inverts.

questions.learning_objective: Identify tibialis posterior as the muscle combining plantarflexion with inversion.

questions.title: Nerves needed for inversion
questions.question: A 47-year-old woman is unable to invert her foot. Which of the following nerves are most likely injured?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Neither superficial nor deep peroneal nerve alone accounts for both invertors — superficial peroneal supplies only evertors (peroneus longus/brevis).
explanations.B: Correct. Inversion depends on tibialis anterior (deep peroneal nerve) and tibialis posterior (tibial nerve); losing both requires injury to both nerves together, so complete loss of inversion points to this pair. A lesion of only one of these two nerves would leave partial inversion intact through the other muscle, so complete loss requires both.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Superficial peroneal supplies evertors, not an invertor, so it is not part of the correct pair.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The plantar nerves supply the sole's intrinsic muscles, not the invertors of the ankle itself.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The obturator nerve has no action on the foot at all.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that complete loss of inversion requires injury to both the deep peroneal nerve (tibialis anterior) and the tibial nerve (tibialis posterior).

questions.title: Sensory loss with impaired dorsiflexion
questions.question: A patient presents with sensory loss on the adjacent sides of the great and second toes and impaired dorsiflexion of the foot. These signs probably indicate damage to which of the following nerves?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The superficial peroneal nerve is not typically associated with the specific first-web-space sensory patch, and its injury does not itself impair dorsiflexion.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The lateral plantar nerve supplies part of the sole, unrelated to this dorsal web space or to dorsiflexion.
explanations.C: Correct. The deep peroneal nerve both drives the whole dorsiflexor group and carries the exact sensory patch described — the adjacent sides of the great and second toes (the first web space) — so both findings together point to it. Recognising that this specific sensory-plus-motor combination localises to one nerve, rather than assuming a root or plexus lesion, is the clinical reasoning this vignette tests.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The sural nerve is purely sensory over the lateral foot and has no dorsiflexion role.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The tibial nerve supplies plantarflexion/inversion and sole sensation, the opposite pattern from what is described.

questions.learning_objective: Combine the deep peroneal nerve's first-web-space sensory field with its dorsiflexor motor role to localise a combined sensory/motor deficit.

questions.title: Weakness in dorsiflexion and inversion (again)
questions.question: A patient experiences weakness in dorsiflexing and inverting the foot. Which of the following muscles is damaged?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Peroneus longus everts and plantarflexes, the opposite pair of actions.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Peroneus brevis also everts, not inverts.
explanations.C: Correct. Tibialis anterior is the only muscle that both dorsiflexes and inverts the foot together. No other listed muscle produces this exact combination, which is why weakness in both movements together should point specifically to tibialis anterior.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Extensor digitorum longus dorsiflexes and helps evert, not invert.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Fibularis (peroneus) tertius dorsiflexes and everts, again not inverting.

questions.learning_objective: Reinforce tibialis anterior as the sole dorsiflexor-invertor of the foot.

questions.title: Nerve for anterolateral leg/ankle sensation
questions.question: A patient involved in a motorcycle wreck has loss of sensation of the skin over the anterolateral leg and ankle. Which of the following nerves is most likely destroyed?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The deep peroneal nerve's cutaneous field is only the first web space, far smaller than the anterolateral leg/ankle described.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The sural nerve covers the posterolateral leg and lateral foot, not the anterolateral leg.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The saphenous nerve covers the medial, not anterolateral, leg.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The posterior tibial nerve has no cutaneous field on the leg itself (its plantar branches cover the sole).
explanations.E: Correct. The superficial peroneal nerve covers the anterolateral leg's lower two-thirds and continues onto the ankle/dorsum, matching the described territory exactly. Recognising the superficial peroneal nerve's broad anterolateral field, distinct from the deep peroneal nerve's tiny web-space patch, is the key discrimination this stem tests.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the superficial peroneal nerve's anterolateral leg and ankle cutaneous field.

questions.title: Muscle flexing the knee and plantarflexing the foot
questions.question: A 14-year-old complains of pain in the knee and ankle joints. Her physician found that the muscle responsible for flexing the leg at the knee joint and plantar flexing the foot is severely weakened. Which of the following muscles was most likely damaged?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Tibialis posterior plantarflexes and inverts but acts only at the ankle, not at the knee.
explanations.B: Correct. Gastrocnemius, arising above the knee, crosses both the knee (weak flexor) and the ankle (strong plantarflexor) — the only muscle among these options that does both. This combination — knee flexion plus ankle plantarflexion together — should point specifically to gastrocnemius rather than to soleus, which shares the ankle action but not the knee-crossing origin.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Soleus plantarflexes the ankle only, having no origin above the knee.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Peroneus longus plantarflexes and everts the ankle but has no knee action.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Flexor digitorum longus plantarflexes the ankle and flexes the toes, but not the knee.

questions.learning_objective: Identify gastrocnemius as the only leg muscle flexing the knee while also plantarflexing the ankle.

questions.title: Sciatic nerve cut — the spared finding
questions.question: A patient was admitted with a penetrating wound at the back of his thigh; examination showed a completely cut sciatic nerve. He will suffer from all the following EXCEPT:

options.A: Paralysis of the muscles of the anterior compartment of the leg
options.B: Paralysis of the muscles of the sole of the foot
options.D: Loss of sensations of the medial aspect of leg

explanations.A: Incorrect (this DOES occur). The anterior compartment (common peroneal division) is paralysed by a complete sciatic cut.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this DOES occur). The sole's muscles (tibial division) are also paralysed.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this DOES occur). Loss of the anterior compartment's dorsiflexors produces foot drop.
explanations.D: Correct. The medial leg is saphenous (femoral-derived) territory, not sciatic, so its sensation is spared even with a complete sciatic nerve transection. Recognising that the saphenous nerve is a femoral-nerve derivative, entirely separate from the sciatic nerve, is what explains why this one strip of skin is spared despite the sciatic nerve being completely cut.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that the medial leg's saphenous (femoral-derived) sensation survives a complete sciatic nerve transection.
